passage:
"They want me to bring my gold bangles on Friday," Ganga said, stirring her tea. "For the new temple fund."

Joseph put his cup down. "Your grandmother's bangles?"

"Swamiji says attachment is the root of suffering. And I already cook there four days a week."

"For free?"

"It's seva, Joseph."

"And your job?"

"I took leave. They said the retreat needs me more." She looked at the table. "They also said not to tell Amma. That family pulls you back down."

Joseph was quiet for a moment. "Ganga, you're not stupid. You went there because you really wanted peace. But gold, free work, keeping it from your mother, that's a lot of asking."

Her eyes filled. "I thought I was the problem."

"You're not. Will you call Amma tonight? And my aunt knows a counsellor who helps people leave groups like this."

Ganga nodded slowly and took out her phone.

qa.q: What was Ganga asked to bring on Friday?
qa.a: Her gold bangles, for the new temple fund.

qa.q: What does Ganga's "I thought I was the problem" suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and confused, blaming her own foolishness for the demands rather than the group making them.

qa.q: What small step did Joseph help Ganga take, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He encouraged her to call her mother that night and see a counsellor, which broke the secrecy and brought in trusted family and outside help.

qa.q: How does Joseph see Ganga's situation?
qa.a: Joseph sees Ganga as a sincere seeker being targeted, and he is worried by the demands for gold, free work and secrecy.

grounding: The dialogue shows demands for donations, unpaid labour and secrecy from family as signs of exploitation, and a friend helping the seeker consult family and outside counsel.

passage:
Looking back, I, Hemant, can see the pattern clearly, though at the time it felt like love.

It started with small things. Stay late after meditation to clean the hall. Then weekends. Then the teacher asked me to move my savings into the ashram's account, "to free you from worry." When I hesitated, a senior member told me my doubt was my ego talking, and that I shouldn't discuss ashram matters outside.

I stopped visiting home. My sister Sonali kept calling anyway. One evening she simply turned up at my room with dal and rice and said, "Bhaiya, you look exhausted. Just tell me what's happening."

I did, all of it, and hearing it out loud frightened me.

She sat with me while I called a family friend who was a lawyer. I stepped back the next week. The shame took longer to leave than I did. Sonali kept reminding me: they looked for sincere people, and I was sincere.

qa.q: What did Sonali bring when she turned up at Hemant's room?
qa.a: She brought dal and rice.

qa.q: What did Hemant feel when he said everything out loud?
qa.a: He felt frightened, and later deeply ashamed, even though at the time the group had felt like love.

qa.q: Which choice helped Hemant most, and why?
qa.a: Telling Sonali everything and calling a family friend who was a lawyer, because it broke the secrecy and brought in trusted family and outside counsel.

qa.q: How does Sonali see what happened to her brother?
qa.a: Sonali sees Hemant as a sincere person who was targeted, not a foolish one, and she worried enough to keep calling and turn up at his room.

grounding: The account shows a young man drawn into unpaid work, handing over savings and secrecy from family, and stepping back with his sister's help and outside advice.

passage:
The first time Wasim went to the Thursday satsang in the lane behind Charminar, an old man pressed a steel glass of hot milk into his hands and said, "You look tired, son. Sit."

After a year alone in the city, it was the first place anyone had noticed that.

Now he went every week. He loved the singing, the shared dinner, the way people remembered his mother's name.

He also kept his Saturday cricket with college friends, and his long calls with Sonali, who teased him about "turning saint."

One week a regular said she was moving to another group closer to home. Wasim braced for frowns. Instead the leader hugged her and said, "Come back for Diwali."

Walking home, Wasim felt something settle. This was a family that let you go. That was exactly why he trusted it.

qa.q: What did the old man give Wasim on the first visit?
qa.a: A steel glass of hot milk.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when the leader hugged the woman who was leaving?
qa.a: He felt relieved and settled, because the group let people go warmly, which made him trust it more.

qa.q: What is Wasim doing that keeps his belonging healthy?
qa.a: He enjoys the satsang but keeps his Saturday cricket and his calls with Sonali, so his life has more than one circle.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Wasim's new routine?
qa.a: Sonali seems glad and relaxed about it, teasing him about "turning saint" rather than worrying.

grounding: The passage shows someone who finds acceptance in a satsang, enjoys it, keeps outside friendships, and sees that the community lets people leave with respect.

passage:
"You're back early," Rashmi said as Chandrika dropped her bag by the door.

"I argued with Didi today. At the discussion."

"The meditation Didi? Oh no. Are you in trouble?"

"That's what I expected. She said anger should always be swallowed. I said sometimes anger tells you something is wrong, like when my manager shouted at the new girl."

"And?"

"Everyone went quiet. Then Didi said, 'That's a fair point. Let's think about it together next week.'" Chandrika laughed. "I nearly cried with relief."

Rashmi grinned. "So they didn't throw you out."

"No. Someone even walked me to the bus and said she agreed with me."

"I like hearing that. You've been so much lighter since you joined."

"I know. But I'm glad I can disagree there. And I'm glad I still have you to tell."

qa.q: What did Didi say after Chandrika disagreed?
qa.a: "That's a fair point. Let's think about it together next week."

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling after the discussion?
qa.a: Chandrika felt huge relief, nearly crying, after fearing trouble for disagreeing and being respected instead.

qa.q: What does Chandrika's evening show about a healthy group?
qa.a: A healthy group lets members disagree and still respects them, and Chandrika keeps outside ties like Rashmi to talk things over.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Chandrika's time with the group?
qa.a: Rashmi is happy for Chandrika, noticing how much lighter things have been since joining, and glad the group did not punish the disagreement.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone who feels accepted in a meditation group, keeps an outside friendship, and finds the group respects disagreement.

passage:
I'm Darshan, and it took me a while to say this plainly: the group was controlling me.

It never looked like force. When I missed a Sunday for my cousin's wedding, Omkar messaged, "We missed your energy. Hope nothing blocks your progress." When my mother fell ill and I skipped two weeks, someone mentioned that "karma has its own timing." They noticed what I ate at office lunches. They asked who my new friends were.

I felt guilty all the time, as if I were letting down a whole family.

What changed things was small. I told Omkar I would come once a month, not every week. My stomach knotted as I typed it. Then I spent that free Sunday playing football with old friends from work, laughing more than I had in a year.

When I finally stopped going, I sent one polite message. I didn't owe them an apology.

qa.q: Why did Darshan miss a Sunday?
qa.a: For a cousin's wedding.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel as the group noticed and commented on every choice?
qa.a: Darshan felt constantly guilty, as if letting down a whole family, and anxious when setting a limit.

qa.q: What small boundary helped Darshan, and why?
qa.a: Going once a month instead of weekly freed time for outside friends, which showed Darshan how much the group had been controlling things.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Darshan's once-a-month message?
qa.a: Omkar may see it as Darshan drifting from progress, since the group treated missing events as a spiritual failing rather than a normal choice.

grounding: The reflective account shows a group using guilt, hints of karma and watching to control a member, and the member setting small boundaries, spending time with outsiders and leaving without shame.

passage:
Team lead's note, design studio, Friday

Pallavi used to be the first to laugh at our Friday lunch. For two months now she has eaten at her desk. Today she told me why, after I asked if she was all right.

She joined a spiritual group last year. Lately, she said, members call her if she misses an evening session, tell her that bad luck follows people who skip, and ask to see her phone "to protect her from negative influences." She said she feels guilty all the time and ashamed to be complaining.

I did not tell her what to believe. I said that care doesn't usually look like checking someone's phone, and that she can step back without being a bad person.

What I did next: I invited her to lunch with the team, and she came. I also gave her the number of the company's counselling line, and she saved it while we sat together.

Chetan

qa.q: What did the group members ask to see?
qa.a: Pallavi's phone, "to protect her from negative influences."

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she told the team lead why she ate alone?
qa.a: She felt guilty all the time and ashamed to be complaining about the group.

qa.q: Which of Chetan's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Inviting Pallavi to lunch with the team gave her time with outsiders, and sharing the counselling line gave her a place to talk freely.

qa.q: How might the group members see Pallavi's lunch with her team?
qa.a: They might frame it as a "negative influence" she should avoid, which is part of how they control her.

grounding: A team lead's note shows a young woman whose group guilts her, hints at punishment and watches her phone, and a colleague helping her keep outside ties and know she can leave.

passage:
For three years Siddiq had cleaned the floors of the small Sufi centre in Toronto every Saturday, learning from the teacher that the soul grows through simple living.

Then Beatriz, who did the centre's accounts, asked him to stay after class. She showed him the statements. The winter coat drive money had gone to a car dealership. The teacher had told everyone the coats came from donors.

Siddiq drove home and sat in the parking lot for an hour. He felt stupid. Then furious. Then, strangely, like grieving a death.

"Was all of it fake?" he asked Beatriz on the phone.

"The teachings helped you stop drinking, right? That was real. You did that."

The next morning they went together to the charity regulator's office with copies of the statements. Siddiq kept the old notebooks of verses. He just stopped reading them in the teacher's voice.

qa.q: Where had the winter coat drive money gone?
qa.a: To a car dealership.

qa.q: What did Siddiq feel as he sat in the parking lot?
qa.a: He felt stupid, then furious, then something like grief, as though someone had died.

qa.q: What did Siddiq get right after the discovery?
qa.a: He reported the wrongdoing with Beatriz and kept the good he had learned separate from the teacher who had misused it.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see Siddiq's question "Was all of it fake?"
qa.a: Beatriz sees his hurt but wants him to know his own change, like stopping drinking, was real and his.

grounding: The passage shows someone discovering that a teacher hides wrongdoing, feeling grief and anger, reporting it, and separating the good learned from the person.

passage:
The community centre kitchen in Indore smelled of cumin and boiling rice. Mahima had come early to help with the free lunch, humming one of the teacher's songs about patience.

Then she heard shouting. The teacher who spoke every Sunday about gentleness had the cook, Anjali, pinned by the wrist against the counter, yelling that the dal was late. Anjali's face was white.

Mahima's legs went cold. "Stop. Let go of her."

The teacher dropped Anjali's wrist and walked out.

Mahima stayed with Anjali, wet a cloth for the red mark on her wrist, and listened. "It's happened before," Anjali whispered. "I need this job."

"This isn't your fault. Will you come with me to the committee office now?"

They went together that morning, and Mahima wrote down what she saw. That night she sat with her song notebook for a long time. The songs had still helped her. The singer had not earned them.

qa.q: What was Anjali yelled at about?
qa.a: The dal being late.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling that night with her song notebook?
qa.a: She felt grief and anger mixed with confusion, since the songs had helped her but the teacher who sang them had hurt someone.

qa.q: What did Mahima do that protected Anjali?
qa.a: She stopped the teacher, stayed with Anjali, told her it wasn't her fault, and went with her to the committee office that same morning to report it.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Mahima stepping in?
qa.a: Anjali may feel frightened for her job but also relieved and less alone, since it had happened before and no one had acted.

grounding: The passage shows someone discovering a teacher lives against their own teaching, feeling grief and anger, reporting the abuse and separating the good learned from the person.

passage:
Pema's train had broken down somewhere outside Siliguri, and her phone kept losing signal. It was the worst possible time for Sumit, her brother, to call.

"Everyone is saying you've joined a cult," he said. "Ama is crying. Pala says if you don't come home on Sunday he'll come and fetch you himself."

Pema felt the old urge to hang up. Instead she pressed the phone to her ear. "Sumit, tell me exactly what worries you. Not what people say. What you've seen."

A pause. "You stopped calling. You sent money to them. You sound different."

"Okay. That's fair." The line crackled. "I stopped calling because you all laughed at me. The money was for the meditation course fee, once. But I hear you."

"Then come home."

"I'll come Sunday. And next month, come with me to one session. See it yourselves. If it's wrong, you'll tell me."

The call dropped. She texted: Sunday. Promise.

qa.q: Where had Pema's train broken down?
qa.a: Somewhere outside Siliguri.

qa.q: What did Pema feel when Sumit first mentioned the cult?
qa.a: She felt a defensive urge to hang up, hurt by the family's laughter and pressure.

qa.q: What did Pema do that could stop both sides hardening?
qa.a: She asked for the specific worries, admitted what was fair, promised to come home, and invited her family to see a session themselves.

qa.q: How does Sumit see Pema's new group?
qa.a: Sumit is anxious that she has been pulled into a cult, because she stopped calling, sent money and sounds different.

grounding: Under the constraint of a broken-down train and bad signal, the passage shows a family fearing a cult and reacting with ridicule and threats, and a daughter who listens to specific concerns, stays in contact and invites them to see the group.

passage:
Mehak came out of her room in Saket with her bag packed for the weekend retreat and found her car keys gone.

Arohi, her mother, stood by the door. "You're not going. Your cousins say those people are brainwashing you."

Mehak's first thought was to shout. She could see it: slammed doors, weeks of silence. She put the bag down instead.

"Mummy, what have the cousins actually told you? Let's sit."

Arohi sat stiffly. "That you give them every weekend. That you don't come to family lunches. That you're always on your phone with them."

Mehak nodded slowly. Two of those were true. "I've missed lunches. I'm sorry. Here's an idea: I'll go this time, but next month, come with me. Meet the teacher. Ask anything."

Arohi looked at her for a long moment and held out the keys. "Next month. And you call me tonight."

"I'll call you tonight," Mehak said.

qa.q: What was missing when Mehak came out of her room?
qa.a: Her car keys.

qa.q: What does Arohi hiding the keys suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Arohi is frightened her daughter is being brainwashed and anxious enough to try to stop her by force.

qa.q: What helped Mehak calm the standoff?
qa.a: She sat down, asked for her mother's specific concerns, admitted what was true, and invited her to meet the teacher next month.

qa.q: How might Mehak see her mother's fear?
qa.a: Mehak sees that part of it is fair, since she has missed family lunches, even though taking the keys felt like force.

grounding: The passage shows a family member who fears a cult and reacts with force, and a young woman who listens to specific concerns, stays in contact and invites her mother to meet the community.

passage:
Gabriel noticed Sofia's apartment in Madrid was nearly empty. The couch, the bookshelf, even the old piano were gone.

"I sold them," she said happily. "The community is building a retreat house. Everything I give helps."

Gabriel felt his chest tighten. He wanted to say, They're using you. He could picture her face closing if he did.

"You look happy," he said instead, and meant it. "What do you love most about them?"

She talked for twenty minutes about the morning silence, the songs, the woman who had held her when her father died.

"Is there anything that ever bothers you there?" he asked.

Sofia hesitated. "Sometimes they get upset when I see old friends."

"Well, this old friend is taking you for churros on Sunday," Gabriel said. "Same as always."

She laughed. On the way out, he told himself: stay close. Keep the door open.

qa.q: What did Sofia sell?
qa.a: Her couch, her bookshelf and her old piano.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling when he saw the empty apartment?
qa.a: He felt worried and tense, his chest tightening at how much Sofia was giving away.

qa.q: Why was asking open questions wiser than saying "They're using you"?
qa.a: Open questions let Sofia talk without defending herself, and one even led her to admit something that bothers her, while an attack would have closed her off.

qa.q: How does Sofia see Gabriel's visit?
qa.a: Sofia seems glad and relaxed with him, happy to share what she loves and pleased to keep their Sunday churros.

grounding: The passage shows a friend worried that someone is giving everything to a group, staying warm, asking open questions and keeping the friendship alive rather than attacking her belief.

passage:
In the Gurugram office, Akash had once been the one who stayed late to help everyone. Now he left at five sharp for his spiritual group, and at lunch he talked about giving the group his whole bonus.

Swati watched him skip a third team dinner. She was worried. She also knew Akash well enough to know that mocking the group would end their friendship.

She caught him at the coffee machine. "Hey. I miss you at dinners. How's your group going?"

He brightened. "They're like family."

"That's lovely. What's a normal week like there?"

He described it. Long evenings. Weekends. "They say doubts mean my ego is fighting."

"And do you have doubts?"

He looked at his cup. "Sometimes."

"You can always tell me about them," Swati said. "No judgement. And come to Friday's dinner. We'll save you a seat."

He came. He stayed an hour.

qa.q: What did Akash say the group tells him about doubts?
qa.a: "They say doubts mean my ego is fighting."

qa.q: What was Swati worried about when Akash skipped a third team dinner?
qa.a: She was anxious that Akash was giving the group all his time and money, and afraid that mocking it would end their friendship.

qa.q: What could Swati keep doing to help Akash?
qa.a: Stay warm, keep asking open questions, and keep inviting him to things, so he has someone to turn to when doubts grow.

qa.q: How might Akash see Swati's question at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Akash seems glad to be asked kindly and safe enough to admit he sometimes has doubts.

grounding: The passage shows a colleague worried about a friend giving his time and money to a group, staying warm, asking open questions and keeping the friendship alive without attacking his belief.

passage:
After the startup folded, Saurabh slept for two days and then started searching.

In six months he tried a silent retreat in Rishikesh, a breathing class in a Bandra studio, a Sunday Bible study with a colleague, and a podcast-famous coach who promised "total awakening in thirty days" for a large fee. He skipped that one.

His sister Sangeeta watched from the sofa of their Mumbai flat. "You're shopping for gods," she teased.

"Maybe," he said. "But I'm checking one thing. Does it make me kinder on a Tuesday? Do I sleep better? Do I shout less at the auto driver?"

The breathing class passed the Tuesday test. The Bible study made him curious but not calmer. The retreat was beautiful and then forgotten by Monday.

"So what's the answer?" Sangeeta asked.

"No answer yet. Just going slowly," he said, and put the kettle on for both of them.

qa.q: What did the coach promise?
qa.a: "Total awakening in thirty days" for a large fee.

qa.q: How does Saurabh feel about his search, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He feels hopeful but cautious, testing each path against ordinary days and admitting he has no answer yet without seeming upset by it.

qa.q: What is wise about Saurabh's "Tuesday test"?
qa.a: It checks teachings against daily life, such as sleep and kindness, and helps him avoid promises of instant change.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see her brother's search?
qa.a: Sangeeta finds it a little amusing, teasing him about shopping for gods, but she stays close and curious.

grounding: The passage shows someone seeking meaning after burnout, trying several paths slowly, testing them against daily life and avoiding promises of instant enlightenment.

passage:
"You've been to four temples, a mosque and a church this month," Kashish said, sliding a plate of samosas across the table. "Are you all right, Wasim?"

"Since Abba died, nothing feels steady. I'm looking for something that does."

"And?"

"The mosque is familiar. The church choir made me cry. A man at the temple said if I paid for a special puja, my grief would lift in a week."

"Did you?"

"No. Grief doesn't lift in a week."

Kashish nodded. "What do you actually want to find?"

Wasim thought. "Something I can still believe on a bad Monday. Not just on a good Sunday."

"Then maybe don't pick yet. Keep going. Keep asking."

"You don't think I'm lost?"

"I think you're looking honestly. That's different."

Wasim picked up a samosa and, for the first time that evening, smiled.

qa.q: What did the man at the temple promise Wasim?
qa.a: That if he paid for a special puja, his grief would lift in a week.

qa.q: What was Wasim worried about when he asked Kashish if he was lost?
qa.a: He was anxious that his searching since Abba died meant something was wrong with him, and he felt unsteady without a clear path.

qa.q: What would you advise Wasim, based on the conversation?
qa.a: Keep searching slowly, test each path against bad days as well as good ones, and avoid anyone promising grief will vanish quickly.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Wasim's many visits?
qa.a: Kashish sees them as honest searching after loss rather than being lost, and encourages him to keep asking.

grounding: The dialogue shows someone seeking meaning after a loss by trying many paths, avoiding promises of a quick fix, and choosing to go slowly and keep questioning.

passage:
Dear diary, Himani here, still fuming at 11 pm.

At the office farewell today Chinmay raised a glass and said the new chief minister was "the only honest man left." I could feel my face go hot. I have read enough about that government's handling of the floods to disagree with every word.

I almost said something nasty. Then I remembered how the last office fight ended, with two people not speaking for a year.

So I asked him what worried him most. He said, "Corruption. My father lost his shop to bribes." I didn't expect that.

We found one thing we both believe: that relief money should reach people. That was it. When a colleague joined in and called my side "traitors," I said, "I'm going to get cake," and left.

I didn't win. But Chinmay said goodbye to me warmly. I'll take that.

qa.q: What did Chinmay say had happened to his father?
qa.a: "My father lost his shop to bribes."

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when Chinmay praised the chief minister?
qa.a: Himani felt angry and hot-faced, tempted to say something nasty.

qa.q: Which steps kept the evening from becoming a fight?
qa.a: Asking what worried Chinmay, finding a shared belief about relief money, and leaving when the talk turned to insults.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the conversation?
qa.a: Chinmay likely felt heard rather than attacked, which is why he said goodbye warmly.

grounding: The diary shows someone angered when a colleague praises a distrusted leader, who asks what worries the colleague, finds shared facts, and disengages when insults begin.

passage:
The flight to Dubai was delayed three hours, and Sabina was stuck at the gate next to Hafsa, her brother's new wife, who was talking about the election back home.

Sabina had already decided people who voted Hafsa's way were stupid. She had said so, loudly, at the wedding. She rolled her eyes now.

Then she remembered her professor's rule: before you disagree, say the other side's best argument so well they'd nod. She had never once tried it.

"Okay," Sabina said. "Let me try. You care about safety at night, and you think that party will get more police on the streets. You're tired of being scared walking home from the station."

Hafsa stared. "Yes. Exactly that."

"I still think they're wrong about a lot. But that's not stupid."

They argued for the next two hours, properly this time. By boarding, Sabina had bought them both tea.

qa.q: How long was the flight to Dubai delayed?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What did Sabina feel when Hafsa said "Yes. Exactly that"?
qa.a: Sabina felt surprised and a little humbled, seeing that the view she had dismissed as stupid came from a real fear.

qa.q: Why did explaining Hafsa's strongest view help?
qa.a: It dropped Sabina's contempt, showed her Hafsa's real grievance, and let them argue honestly instead of insulting each other.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Sabina after the gate conversation?
qa.a: Hafsa may feel understood for the first time, after being called stupid at the wedding, and more willing to talk.

grounding: Under a long flight delay, the passage shows someone who sees the other side as stupid, then states their strongest view before disagreeing and discovers a real grievance.

passage:
Saurabh's building in Pune had a residents' chat that had turned into a political battlefield. He had been typing sarcastic replies for weeks. "Only fools would believe that," he had written that morning, about Vandana from the fourth floor.

In the evening he met her at the lift, carrying groceries.

"You think I'm a fool," she said, not angrily. Just tired.

He felt heat in his face. "I, well, the post was..."

"My husband's factory closed last year. The other side promised to reopen it. I'm not stupid. I'm scared."

The lift was slow. Saurabh made himself say it back. "So you're voting for the plan that sounds like it will bring the jobs back, because you're worried about your family's income."

"Yes."

"I still don't trust their plan. But I get why you do."

Vandana nodded. They rode up in quiet. That night Saurabh deleted his morning post.

qa.q: What had Saurabh written about Vandana that morning?
qa.a: "Only fools would believe that."

qa.q: What did Saurabh feel when Vandana said "You think I'm a fool"?
qa.a: Saurabh felt ashamed and embarrassed, heat rising in his face as he struggled to explain.

qa.q: What changed Saurabh's contempt?
qa.a: Hearing Vandana's real worry and saying her view back fairly showed him a grievance he had been blind to.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Saurabh's post?
qa.a: Vandana felt hurt and tired by it, because it called her a fool when she was actually frightened for her family.

grounding: The passage shows someone who treats the other side as fools, is confronted with a real grievance, and restates the other person's strongest view before disagreeing.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel after reading Gurpreet's messages?
qa.a: He felt hurt and stung, his heart still thudding after he put the phone down.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arnab keep his dignity?

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet call the insult "a joke"?

grounding: The chat shows someone dismissed as brainwashed and anti-national who states his view briefly, refuses the label and ends the talk calmly without needing to win.

passage:
At the tea stall by the bus stand in Sangli, the talk had turned to the coming election. Suraj said quietly that he thought the new canal project had been badly planned.

Rukmini, who ran the stall, snorted. "Listen to him. Two years in Pune and he comes back brainwashed. These city boys forget their own village."

The old men laughed. Suraj felt it land in his stomach. For a moment he wanted to list every report he had read.

He set his glass down. "Rukmini-akka, I grew up four houses from here. I think the canal should reach the eastern fields too. That's all."

"See? Anti-village."

"You can call it what you like. I know what I think." He counted out his coins, smiled at her, and said, "Your tea is still the best in Sangli."

He walked to the bus with his face burning and his back straight.

qa.q: Where did Suraj grow up?
qa.a: Four houses from the tea stall.

qa.q: What does Suraj's burning face as he walks away suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he still felt stung and embarrassed by Rukmini's label, even though he kept his calm.

qa.q: What did Suraj get right in responding to the label?
qa.a: He stated his view in one line, refused to be defined as anti-village, and left calmly and politely instead of arguing.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Suraj's calm answer?
qa.a: Rukmini may be a little surprised that he didn't fight back, and perhaps softened by his compliment about her tea.

grounding: The passage shows a young man dismissed as brainwashed and anti-village who states his view briefly, refuses the label and ends the exchange calmly with dignity.
